dun_dolphins.text: There are bottlenose dolphins in the Tay. You see them off Broughty Ferry, along the coast there, leaping in the river mouth. Bring a flask. Bring patience.
Grey seals and common seals too, on the sandbanks at Tentsmuir across the water. The Tay is busier than the bridge.

dun_comic_fan.text: Dundee's been making comics for kids for nearly a hundred years. Cowboys who eat cow pie, menaces with catapults, bash street bands of rascals. Generations of British kids learnt to read from them.
The statue's Desperate Dan. He's so strong he shaves with a blowtorch. My dad says I'm not allowed to try that.

dun_millworker.text: My granny was a spinner in a jute mill. She started at twelve. The men stayed home and minded the bairns, so they called them kettle bilers, kettle boilers. Dundee was a women's town.
The mill chimneys were everywhere. Cox's Stack at Lochee is still standing, nearly three hundred feet tall, like a bell tower for jute.

dun_law_walker.text: Up the Law every morning. You can see right over the Tay to Fife, and on a clear day out to the sea. Behind you, the Sidlaw Hills.
Dundonians say 'eh' for 'I' and 'pehs' for 'pies'. A steak peh, please. Practise that. You'll need it at the football.

then.text: The lamps hang over the water where the old girders stood. A whistle, very faint, from a long way off. It is waiting for you.

else.text: The wind gets up off the Tay. Out on the water, between the old stumps, two lamps are moving, steady as a train. There are no rails there. There haven't been since 1879.
The lamps come closer. Iron and steam and something lonelier than either. It stops at the end of the quay as if it had always meant to.

then.text: The lamps dim to a warm, contented glow. Whatever was crossing the Tay has, at last, got to the other side. It seems to have decided that the other side is you.

else.text: The lamps flicker, and fade back over the water towards the stumps. A long, low whistle. It will cross again.
Out on the water, the stumps of the old bridge stand in a line, like the posts of a fence nobody finished. Folk say a ghost train crosses here, but only at night.
